new.title: Pass under the Sabelspoort
new.desc: Arnhem once had four medieval city gates; the Sabelspoort is the only one still standing. Its baroque front dates from 1642 and it sits right by the Rhine, a short walk from the bridge.
new.tip: Combine it with the John Frost bridge and the river quay; the gate looks best from the Rijnkade side.

new.title: Go down into Arnhem's medieval cellars
new.desc: Under the shopping streets near the Rhine lies a network of around three dozen vaulted cellars where merchants once stored their goods. A walk through them shows the city that existed long before the war rebuilt its surface.
new.tip: The entrance is on Oude Oeverstraat; the route stays cool all year, so bring a layer even in summer.

new.title: Drink a beer in the old post office
new.desc: The grand neo-Gothic post office on Jansplein now pours beer and wine instead of stamping letters. 't Taphuys keeps the high ceilings and big windows of the old counter hall.
new.tip: Pick something from the long draft list and look up: the building's original details are the real show.

new.title: Eat hyper-local at LOCALS
new.desc: The restaurant in Hotel Haarhuis next to the station cooks with produce from the region and grows part of it in its own vertical farm. It is Arnhem's showcase for Gelderland flavours.
new.tip: Finish with a drink at BLOU, the rooftop bar of the same hotel, for a view over the city.

new.title: Buy bread from the Sonsbeek water mill
new.desc: At the edge of Sonsbeek park a working water mill still grinds grain, and the bakery beside it sells organic flour and baked goods made from it.
new.tip: Grab something warm and eat it on the grass by the mill pond before heading up into the park.

new.title: Play with water at the Watermuseum
new.desc: In a country that lives below sea level, this hands-on museum in Sonsbeek explains where water comes from and where it goes, sewers included. Lots of buttons, pumps and splashing.
new.tip: Locals like the lawns outside for a picnic afterwards; it sits right next to the Sonsbeek water mill.

new.title: Peek inside Huis Zypendaal
new.desc: Next door to busy Sonsbeek, Park Zypendaal is the quieter sibling, with ponds and an 18th-century country house whose ground floor you can visit. The park counts ten national monuments.
new.tip: Walk from Sonsbeek over the Zijpendaalseweg; the house is at its best seen across the pond in front.

new.title: Touch the Roman wall inside De Bastei
new.desc: Roman Nijmegen, Noviomagus, lies mostly buried, but in De Bastei you walk past a Roman gate and wall and climb into the 16th-century Stratemakerstoren. The same building holds a natural history show about the region's landscape.
new.tip: It sits below the Valkhof hill on the river side, so pair it with the Valkhof park and the Waalkade.

new.title: Find the Kruittoren in Kronenburgerpark
new.desc: This park on the old city edge hides the 1425 Kruittoren (powder tower) and surviving stretches of the medieval wall between its ponds and lawns.
new.tip: Bring a picnic; locals use the park as their back garden on sunny afternoons.

new.title: Climb the Stevenskerk tower
new.desc: The Gothic Stevenskerk dominates the old town, and on selected days in the warm season you can climb its tower for a view over the Waal and the rooftops. Inside lies the tomb of Catherine of Bourbon.
new.tip: Enter the church square through the Kerkboog, the archway from the Grote Markt; the church itself is free.

new.title: Order kaasgehakt at De Plak
new.desc: Eetcafé De Plak on Bloemerstraat is an institution of Nijmegen's alternative scene, famous for its kaasgehakt, a cheese-filled meatball.
new.tip: It is popular with students and fills up fast in the evening; come early or be ready to wait at the bar.

new.title: Explore the dark at muZIEum
new.desc: This museum lets you experience the world as blind and visually impaired people do, guided through a pitch-dark expedition by someone who knows it best.
new.tip: Book ahead; there is also an augmented-reality walk through town that starts here.

new.title: Eat pancakes on the Waal
new.desc: The Pannenkoekenboot sails out from the Waalkade for a cruise with as many Dutch pancakes as you can manage, while the bridges and the skyline slide by.
new.tip: Book in advance, especially at weekends; sit by a window on the river side.

new.title: Ride back in time at Velorama
new.desc: The national bicycle museum on the Waalkade shows how the Dutch fell for the bike, from wooden balance bikes to towering high-wheelers.
new.tip: Afterwards walk the Waalkade terraces east towards the Valkhof for the river view.

new.title: Meet the Face of Nijmegen
new.desc: On the river island Veur-Lent a giant metal face stares back at the city. The sculpture by Andreas Hetfeld is inspired by a Roman cavalry mask found in Nijmegen.
new.tip: Cross the Snelbinder bike and foot bridge beside the railway bridge; the view back to the old town is the best skyline shot in the city.

new.title: Stand where the war ended in Wageningen
new.desc: At Hotel de Wereld in Wageningen the German commander in the Netherlands capitulated to the Canadians on 5 May 1945; the papers were signed next door the following day because there was no typewriter.
new.tip: Come on 5 May, when the town's Liberation Day celebrations centre on this square. Wageningen is a short bus ride from Ede-Wageningen station.

new.title: Taste student-town beer in Wageningen
new.desc: Wageningen's university crowd keeps a lively bar scene; the Stadsbrouwerij brews its own beer in a lane right off the market square.
new.tip: Then try the beer list at De Vlaamsche Reus on the main square, which counts well over a hundred bottles.

new.title: Visit Kasteel Doorwerth on the Rhine
new.desc: This moated castle in the Rhine floodplain west of Arnhem was badly damaged in 1944 and restored over decades. Today it holds furnished historic rooms and museums on hunting and nature.
new.tip: Look for the huge black locust tree by the entrance, said to be the oldest in the country; the riverside walk to Oosterbeek starts nearby.

new.title: Eat Veluwe game at Planken Wambuis
new.desc: A forest inn from 1926 between Ede and Arnhem, with a hunting-lodge interior and a menu built around venison and other Veluwe game.
new.tip: Walk or cycle the Ginkelse Heide or the Planken Wambuis woods first; autumn is the high season for game.

new.title: Go underground at Museonder
new.desc: In the heart of De Hoge Veluwe park, Museonder shows what happens beneath the forest floor. The roots of a 135-year-old tree hang over your head in the middle of the hall.
new.tip: It is part of the visitor centre, where you can also pick up a white bike; entry is included with the park ticket.

new.title: Find Harderwijk's Vischpoort
new.desc: This late-medieval gate on the old Zuiderzee shore of Harderwijk once had fishing boats moored beside it to sell their catch. It is one of the few pieces left of the city walls.
new.tip: Walk on to the lakeside boulevard; Harderwijk is a short train ride from Amersfoort or Zwolle.

new.title: Walk the grid streets of Elburg
new.desc: Elburg on the old Zuiderzee coast was laid out on a strict grid in 1392 and still keeps its walls, moat and casemates. The Vischpoort survived because it doubled as a coastal light.
new.tip: The casemates can be visited in summer; start at the VVV on Jufferenstraat for a walking map.

new.title: Find William and Anna in Buren
new.desc: In the tiny fortified town of Buren, William of Orange married Anna van Buren in the Sint-Lambertuskerk in 1551, which is why the royal family still carries the title of count of Buren. A statue of the couple stands by the church.
new.tip: Visit Museum Buren & Oranje in the old town hall and the Prins van Oranje mill on the ramparts; in spring the orchards around town bloom.

new.title: Cycle through the Betuwe blossom
new.desc: The Betuwe is the fruit basket of the Netherlands, and in spring its apple, pear and cherry orchards turn white and pink. The yearly Bloesemtocht route usually starts in Geldermalsen.
new.tip: Check the regional blossom barometer before you go; bloom peaks vary per year. Farm stands along the way sell fresh fruit and juice.

new.title: Watch the Fruitcorso in Tiel
new.desc: Every September since 1961, floats covered in fruit and vegetables parade through Tiel, the jam town of the Betuwe. Tiel's mascot Flipje, born as a jam advert, is everywhere.
new.tip: Look for the Flipje mosaic at the Waterpoort by the Waal; the free Appelpop festival is held around the same time.

new.title: See the leaning tower of Acquoy
new.desc: The 15th-century church tower in the hamlet of Acquoy on the Linge leans almost as much as Pisa's. Builders already tried to correct the tilt halfway up, and you can still see the kink.
new.tip: Make it a stop on a Betuwe bike ride along the Linge; the village is tiny, so the tower is hard to miss.

new.title: Circle the bastions of Zaltbommel
new.desc: Zaltbommel's star-shaped ramparts with seven bastions and a wide moat are still easy to trace, now turned into parks. The tall Sint-Maartenskerk and the Gasthuistoren with its bulb top rise above the walled town.
new.tip: Approach on foot or by bike over the Waal bridge: the view of the water tower, the walls and the church behind them is the classic one.

new.title: Stroll through tiny Bronkhorst
new.desc: With barely a hundred or so residents, Bronkhorst on the IJssel ranks among the smallest towns with city rights in the country. Its cobbled lanes, castle mound and little chapel make a perfect short walk.
new.tip: Climb the castle hill, the only trace left of the medieval castle, then look out over the IJssel floodplains.

new.title: Tour Kasteel Huis Bergh in 's-Heerenberg
new.desc: This moated castle in the Achterhoek holds the largest private collection of early Italian art in the Netherlands, along with manuscripts, ivory and portraits of the counts of Bergh.
new.tip: Stroll the castle garden, restored to its 1727 layout; you can even sleep in one of the towers.

new.title: Listen to the monks at Sint Willibrordsabdij
new.desc: In the Slangenburg woods just outside Doetinchem, Benedictine monks keep the hours of prayer. The chapel is open all day and anyone can quietly join a service.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk past nearby Kasteel de Slangenburg; the abbey is a short bike ride from Doetinchem station.

new.title: Taste Walterbier in Doetinchem
new.desc: The Stadsbrouwerij Doetinchem brews Walterbier right in the centre of the Achterhoek's main town, and opens up for brewery tours.
new.tip: Monthly public tours run on a Sunday afternoon; otherwise just drop in for a glass in the old centre.

new.title: Meet young Mondriaan in Winterswijk
new.desc: Long before his grids of red, yellow and blue, Piet Mondriaan grew up in this house in Winterswijk. Villa Mondriaan shows his early landscapes next to work by other artists.
new.tip: It is a short walk from Winterswijk station; afterwards cycle out into the hedged farmland that he painted.

new.title: Have lunch at Berenschot's watermill
new.desc: South of Winterswijk, a water mill from 1652 on the edge of a small nature reserve now houses a restaurant. Its wheel still turns on the stream outside.
new.tip: Cycle there from Winterswijk through the Achterhoek coulisse landscape of hedges and small fields.
